questions.q: Why can't a QPU decide on its own to run a different circuit based on the measurement results it just produced?
options: A QPU executes a fixed circuit and returns measurement counts; it has no control-flow capability to branch on results itself -- that decision has to be made by classical code
QPUs are too slow to make decisions in real time
Cloud providers disable branching for billing reasons
QPUs can branch on results, but only IBM's hardware supports it
questions.explain: A QPU prepares a state, evolves it under a fixed gate sequence, and measures it -- it has no mechanism to inspect results and branch. Deciding the next circuit is always a classical responsibility.

questions.q: In a typical hybrid application, roughly what fraction of the code never touches the QPU directly?
options: Over 95% -- almost all of it is classical data prep, control flow, optimization, and result handling
About 50%, split evenly between quantum and classical code
Less than 10% -- most of the logic has to run on the QPU
0% -- every line of a hybrid application executes on quantum hardware
questions.explain: The QPU is called for a narrow set of operations (state preparation/evolution/measurement); everything else -- data prep, the optimizer, convergence checks, cost tracking, error handling -- is ordinary classical code, which is the overwhelming majority of the codebase.

questions.q: According to the lesson, which of these is something current quantum hardware is actually good at?
options: Evaluating the expectation value of a quantum observable (like a Hamiltonian) for certain hard-to-simulate systems
Reading a file from disk
Printing a result to a log
Running an if/else branch based on a prior measurement
questions.explain: Evaluating observable expectation values for specific classically-intractable systems is one of the few things current QPUs are suited for; file I/O, logging, and branching are classical operations a QPU cannot perform.

questions.q: What is the practical consequence of treating the classical control loop, not the QPU, as 'the application'?
options: Engineering priorities correctly shift toward classical orchestration correctness and cost/latency budgeting first, with circuit design as one bounded component
It means the QPU no longer needs to be tested
It means cost and latency budgets become irrelevant
It means you should write all quantum circuits in classical languages
questions.explain: Framing the classical loop as the application correctly prioritizes the orchestration, cost, and latency concerns that determine whether a hybrid system is production-viable -- exactly the focus of Chapters 2 through 5 of this course.

questions.q: A colleague wants an architecture where the QPU 'decides when the job is done' without classical involvement. What is the direct flaw in this plan?
options: A QPU has no way to evaluate a convergence condition or decide to stop iterating -- that check has to be made by classical code reading the returned measurement counts
There is no flaw; this is exactly how production VQE systems are built today
QPUs can do this, but only on annealing hardware, not gate-based hardware
This is flawed only because of cost, not because of any technical limitation
questions.explain: Deciding whether a result has converged requires inspecting the result and comparing it against a threshold -- a control-flow operation no current QPU can perform. The classical layer must own convergence checks, as covered later in the variational loop pattern lesson.
